cards.body:
Repeated flooding on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach is raising concerns among business owners, and the city says a permanent fix could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete. Wednesday's storm flooded the street so severely that water reached knee height in the middle of the road, according to Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, who called it one of the worst floodings he has seen in 20 years.

 The flooding has become a recurring problem tied to daily afternoon thunderstorms. Ocean Drive also flooded on Monday. Aubrey Moxley, who works at Allure Gallery across the street, said the entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain this week. The flooding creates dangerous conditions for employees and threatens to cripple businesses by preventing customers from reaching the beach and shops along the strip.

 The City of Vero Beach Public Works Department said pump stations and drainage infrastructure are working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. Recent storms exceeded that capacity, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour. To fix the flooding, staff said the city would need to rebuild the road and make drainage improvements.

 The city has no improvement project planned for Ocean Drive at this time. Olsen expressed concern about what a major storm could bring to ground-level businesses along the street and questioned where the city draws the line between cost and damage to local businesses.

cards.body:
Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, sent WPTV a video of the flooding on Ocean Drive after Wednesday's storm. He said it was among the worst he has seen. Olsen said he has been at the location for 20 years and Wednesday was probably one of the worst floodings he has seen. The water level was high. When Olsen walked out into the middle of the street, the water was up to his knees. Wednesday was not the first time this week the road flooded. The same thing happened on Monday.

Olsen said the flooding has become a recurring problem tied to the area's daily weather pattern. Every afternoon they get a thunderstorm, and every afternoon they possibly will end up dealing with flooding. Across the street, Aubrey Moxley and Leah Trodglen work at Allure Gallery. Moxley said the flooding builds quickly. It doesn't matter how long it rains for, the water is collecting. The entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain. Moxley said the flooding is a threat to businesses along the strip because customers can't go to the beach or come and shop.

The City of Vero Beach Public Works Department said the pump stations and other drainage infrastructure were working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. The most recent storms exceeded that, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour. To fix the flooding, staff said it would require rebuilding the road and making drainage improvements, a project that could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete. Public works staff said there is no improvement project planned for Ocean Drive at this time.

hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.

The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project. The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases: 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility's operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

Currently, Vero Beach's combined bill of $83.54 falls below the regional average of $89.47 for similar usage. However, once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach's $107.30 bill will exceed several neighboring utilities. Fort Pierce Utilities Authority currently charges $95.76 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level. Indian River County Sewer bills $67.70 for comparable service. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. New rates take effect Oct. 1, with subsequent annual adjustments each Oct.

The City of Vero Beach Public Works Department acknowledged that fixing repeated flooding on Ocean Drive would require a multimillion-dollar road rebuild and drainage improvements, but no project is planned for the street. Public works staff said the existing pump stations and drainage infrastructure are working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour, while recent storms delivered 2 or more inches in an hour. Staff said a permanent fix would take years to complete.

Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, said Wednesday's flooding was among the worst he has seen in 20 years. Olsen said the water reached his knees when he walked into the middle of the street. The street also flooded Monday, and Olsen said flooding has become a recurring problem tied to daily afternoon thunderstorms.

Aubrey Moxley, who works at Allure Gallery across the street, said the entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain. Moxley said the flooding threatens businesses because customers cannot reach shops or the beach. Olsen said he drove an employee to their car through deep water and nearly lost his own vehicle. He said ground-level businesses would flood in a major storm and the city needs to address the problem.

hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested a Fort Pierce man Wednesday evening after a hit-and-run crash on SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road in Palm City led to a two-hour search through swamps and dense woods. Likenson Daceus was captured a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands after fleeing on foot from a head-on collision that left another driver with minor injuries.

The incident began when the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission alerted the Martin County Sheriff's Office about a man suspected of stealing palmetto berries from the Savannah Preserve. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but Daceus fled. He then crashed head-on into another vehicle and left a juvenile in his car before running on foot through the Wind Stone community.

Multiple agencies including MCSO, FWC, and Port St. Lucie police utilized road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units to track Daceus through dense brush and swamp conditions. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said deputies tracked him through neighborhood yards into the swamp after finding his hat. Neighbors near Wind Stone sheltered in place during the search. Resident Tanya Talanczuck said the heavy police presence Tuesday caught the neighborhood by surprise.

Daceus is charged with one felony and a misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Budensiek warned anyone considering fleeing into the county's natural areas. "We're not afraid of snakes, alligators, swamps, oceans, sharks. We're from here. So if you're gonna come here to our county and think you're gonna hide in our swamps, we're gonna come in there and get you," Budensiek said.

Fort Pierce resident Likenson Daceus was arrested after leading multiple law enforcement agencies through more than two hours of searching dense woods and swamp in Palm City, following a hit-and-run crash that left another driver with minor injuries. The manhunt began after Daceus fled a traffic stop and crashed head-on into another vehicle on SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road, then abandoned a juvenile in his car before running into natural lands near the Wind Stone community. Deputies captured Daceus a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands. He faces one felony charge and one misdemeanor charge for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest.

The incident started when the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission alerted the Martin County Sheriff's Office about a man suspected of stealing palmetto berries from the Savannah Preserve. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but Daceus fled. After the crash, the police report says he left a juvenile in his car before taking off on foot.

The manhunt involved multiple agencies including the Martin County Sheriff's Office, FWC, and Port St. Lucie police, utilizing road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said neighbors pointed deputies to the last location they saw Daceus running, and canine deputies picked up a track and found his hat. Budensiek said deputies tracked him through dense woods, through a backyard, and into the swamp. Neighbors near Wind Stone, including resident Tanya Talanczuck, sheltered in place during the search.

Sheriff Budensiek warned anyone considering fleeing into the county's natural areas. "We're not afraid of snakes, alligators, swamps, oceans, sharks — we're from here. So if you're gonna come here to our county and think you're gonna hide in our swamps, we're gonna come in there and get you," Budensiek said. He added that once Daceus hurt one of their people, "it was game on for us," and that he believed Daceus would have done anything to get away and posed a danger to the community.

hero.body:
Recurring flooding on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach is crippling businesses and the city says a permanent fix could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete, with no improvement project currently planned for the road. The City of Vero Beach Public Works Department told WPTV that fixing the flooding would require rebuilding the road and making drainage improvements. Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, said Wednesday's storm brought some of the worst flooding he has seen in 20 years, with water reaching his knees in the middle of the street.

The flooding struck Ocean Drive twice this week, on Monday and again Wednesday. Aubrey Moxley, who works at Allure Gallery across the street from Waldo's, said the entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain. Olsen said the flooding has become a recurring problem tied to daily afternoon thunderstorms. He drove an employee to their car because the water was so deep he almost lost his own vehicle.

Public works staff said the pump stations and other drainage infrastructure were working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. The most recent storms exceeded that capacity, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour. Moxley said the flooding is a threat to businesses along the strip because customers cannot reach the beach or come shop, calling it potentially crippling for Ocean Drive businesses.

Olsen said he is worried about what a major storm could bring to ground-level businesses and called the situation unacceptable, saying it needs to be addressed by the city. He acknowledged the scale of the challenge as a big financial endeavor but questioned where to draw the line between cost and damage to local businesses. Leah Trodglen also works at Allure Gallery. Moxley said she has never seen the street flood the way it has this past week.

hero.angle: Lead with the newly leaked grand jury report confirming $10 million in Medicaid settlement funds was misappropriated through Hope Florida into political committees, and David Jolly's call to reopen the investigation — set against DeSantis' and Uthmeier's denials.

hero.body:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly called Thursday for the Hope Florida investigation to be reopened after a newly leaked grand jury report concluded that $10 million in taxpayer money was misappropriated for political purposes. The report, obtained by CBS Miami, details how money from a $67 million Medicaid settlement between Florida and healthcare company Centene moved through Hope Florida and ultimately reached political groups.

 The grand jury found that $10 million from the settlement went to the Hope Florida Foundation, a program championed by first lady Casey DeSantis that connects people in need with charities, churches, and other community organizations. The decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida was the original misappropriation, according to the report.

 The grand jury traced how the money was then divided into two $5 million grants to separate nonprofits. According to the report, $8.5 million eventually went to Keep Florida Clean, a political committee chaired by James Uthmeier, now the state's Attorney General and then Governor Ron DeSantis' chief of staff. The committee subsequently sent $7 million to the Republican Party of Florida.

 The grand jury included a flow chart tracing the money from Centene through Hope Florida and the nonprofits into political organizations. While the report says jurors could plainly see taxpayer money was misused for political purposes, the grand jury did not recommend criminal charges. The report says jurors could not prove who made the original decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida, and no one involved took responsibility for making that decision.

 Governor DeSantis strongly disputed the grand jury's conclusions at a press conference Thursday in Lake City. He said no Medicaid money was diverted and argued the $10 million was part of a private contribution tied to the settlement. He accused critics of using the controversy to attack his wife and called the scrutiny politically motivated.

 Uthmeier also pushed back Thursday, calling the investigation a politically motivated witch hunt. The grand jury recommended that lawmakers change state law to prevent a similar situation from happening again. Among its recommendations are clearer rules for how state-affiliated nonprofits can use taxpayer money, requirements to track and monitor such spending, and consequences for violations.

 Jolly said if elected governor, he would use the powers of the governor's office to pursue additional answers about who made the decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida and how the money ultimately reached political organizations. The grand jury report noted that virtually everyone involved was a lawyer, and many witnesses said they acted based on the advice of other lawyers, which made criminal prosecution more difficult. DeSantis said the only crime that was apparent was whoever leaked the grand jury report.

cards.body:
New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023, both hired through no-bid contracts, even as the school maintains a 13-member in-house marketing and communications team, public records show. The spending comes as Governor Ron DeSantis has defended more than $60 million in state funding to transform the small liberal arts college of about 1,000 students away from what he calls woke indoctrination. More than $400,000 has gone to TMF Communications, run by Taryn Fenske, a former spokesperson for both New College President Richard Corcoran during his time as Florida's education commissioner and for Governor DeSantis. Fenske also led DeSantis' presidential super PAC before securing her no-bid contract with New College in July 2023. According to college invoices, Fenske has been paid upwards of $15,000 per month, plus travel expenses, to help improve the school's brand, create proactive messaging, and produce promotional videos.

Another nearly $400,000 has gone to a second firm, Evandr.co, a company run by Katy Saeger, a California PR consultant who describes her crisis communication services as behind the scenes and discreet. Her no-bid contract with New College, signed in November 2023, is worth just over $12,000 per month, plus nearly $30,000 in back pay. This January, Evandr.co's monthly fees were reduced to $5,000. Last year, a state audit found New College, while the smallest public college in Florida's university system, is also the most financially inefficient. According to the report, it costs nearly three times as much to earn a degree at New College than UF, the state's largest university. Spending per student at New College during FY 2024 was $83,207, nearly double spending at UF and the highest among all public universities in the state.

New College Professor Sarah Hernandez said faculty have recently been asked to make budget cuts, making the continued spending for outside PR especially difficult to understand. New College spokesman Jamie Miller defended the outsourced PR hires, saying the school, like many colleges and universities across Florida, works with outside vendors in a variety of operational areas, including communications and marketing. Ben Wilcox, who leads Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, said the contracts look bad to the public and resemble sweetheart deals given to former allies who are being rewarded for their loyalty.
cards.headline: New College of Florida spends nearly $1 million on outside PR consultants despite 13-member in-house team
cards.teaser: New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023, both hired through no-bid contracts, even as the school maintains a 13-member in-house marketing and communications team.

New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023 through no-bid contracts, public records show. The spending comes as faculty have been asked to make budget cuts and a state audit last year found New College, while the smallest public college in Florida's university system, is also the most financially inefficient. According to the audit, it costs nearly three times as much to earn a degree at New College than at the University of Florida, the state's largest university. Spending per student at New College during fiscal year 2024 was $83,207, nearly double spending at UF and the highest among all public universities in the state.

More than $400,000 has gone to TMF Communications, run by Taryn Fenske, a former spokesperson for both New College President Richard Corcoran during his time as Florida's education commissioner and for Governor Ron DeSantis. New College spokesman Jamie Miller defended the outsourced PR hires, saying the school works with outside vendors in a variety of operational areas, including communications and marketing. President Richard Corcoran said the consultants were hired when the school's own PR department wasn't fully staffed and the college was facing state and federal investigations. Ben Wilcox, who leads Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, said the contracts should raise concerns for taxpayers. cards.body:
Florida homeowners are finding that credit reports and third-party data profiles are quietly driving insurance premiums higher, adding a new dimension to the state's insurance affordability crisis. A Palm Beach County homeowner named Todd told WPTV in an email that his insurer raised his premium based on a LexisNexis rating in his credit report. In July, a Delray Beach driver alerted WPTV to how a detailed credit and data report was affecting a premium quote.

Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said the information is used to determine the risk of each policyholder and set rates either higher or lower. Norberg said data companies including credit bureaus now have extensive information on consumers and can pull credit scores based on the type of underwriting being done, whether auto or property. Different insurance companies have different ways of interpreting the data in the reports, but most use it to assess the risk of each policyholder, Norberg said.
cards.headline: Florida homeowners learn credit reports and data profiles affect insurance premiums
cards.teaser: Homeowners across Florida are discovering that credit reports and third-party data profiles are being used to set their insurance rates. The practice is adding to affordability concerns as insurers use detailed personal information to assess policyholder risk.

hero.body:
A newly leaked grand jury report concluded that $10 million in taxpayer money from a Medicaid settlement was misappropriated for political purposes through the Hope Florida Foundation, prompting Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly to call for reopening the investigation. The sealed report, obtained Wednesday by CBS Miami, details how the money moved from a $67 million settlement between Florida and healthcare company Centene into Hope Florida and ultimately into political organizations. The grand jury wrote that jurors could plainly see taxpayer money was misused for political purposes, though no criminal charges were recommended. Governor Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier both denied wrongdoing Thursday, with DeSantis calling the leak itself the only apparent crime and Uthmeier labeling the investigation a politically motivated witch hunt.

The grand jury report says the decision to send the $10 million from the Centene settlement to Hope Florida was the original misappropriation. Hope Florida is a program championed by first lady Casey DeSantis that connects people in need with charities, churches, and other community organizations. The money was then divided into two $5 million grants to separate nonprofits. According to the report, $8.5 million eventually went to Keep Florida Clean, a political committee chaired by Uthmeier, who was then serving as DeSantis' chief of staff. The committee subsequently sent $7 million to the Republican Party of Florida.

The grand jury did not recommend criminal charges because jurors could not prove who made the original decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida, and no one involved took responsibility for making that decision. The report says virtually everyone involved was a lawyer, and many witnesses said they acted based on the advice of other lawyers. The grand jury said that made criminal prosecution more difficult. The report included a flow chart tracing the money from Centene through Hope Florida and the nonprofits into political organizations.

Jolly said Thursday that if elected governor, he would reopen the investigation and pursue additional fact-finding. DeSantis disputed the grand jury's conclusion at a press conference in Lake City, saying no Medicaid money was diverted and arguing the $10 million was part of a private contribution tied to the settlement. He accused critics of using the controversy to attack his wife and called the scrutiny politically motivated. The grand jury also recommended that lawmakers change state law to prevent a similar situation, including clearer rules for how state-affiliated nonprofits can use taxpayer money, requirements to track and monitor such spending, and consequences for violations.

hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Likenson Daceus, a Fort Pierce man, after a two-hour search through dense woods and swamp in Palm City natural lands following a hit-and-run crash Wednesday evening. Daceus fled on foot after crashing head-on into another vehicle at SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road, leaving the driver with minor injuries and abandoning a juvenile in his car.

The incident began when the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission alerted the Martin County Sheriff's Office about a man suspected of stealing palmetto berries from the Savannah Preserve. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but Daceus fled. After the crash, deputies tracked Daceus through the Wind Stone community and into swampland a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands.

Multiple agencies including MCSO, FWC, and Port St. Lucie police deployed road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said deputies tracked Daceus through dense brush after neighbors pointed to where they last saw him running. Deputies found his hat and followed tracks through backyards into the swamp before making the arrest.

Daceus faces charges of one felony and one misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Tanya Talanczuck, a resident near the Wind Stone community, said she sheltered in place during the search and was relieved by the quick arrest. Sheriff Budensiek warned anyone considering fleeing into the county's natural areas that deputies are not afraid of snakes, alligators, or swamps.
hero.headline: Hit-and-run suspect arrested after two-hour manhunt through Palm City swamps

hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Likenson Daceus after a two-hour search through dense woods and swamp in Palm City that began Tuesday when he fled the scene of a head-on collision on SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road. Daceus is charged with one felony and one misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Deputies captured him a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands near the Wind Stone community.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission first alerted the Martin County Sheriff's Office about a man suspected of stealing palmetto berries from the Savannah Preserve. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but Daceus fled. He then crashed head-on into another vehicle, leaving the driver with minor injuries. The police report says he left a juvenile in his car before taking off on foot.

The manhunt involved multiple agencies including MCSO, FWC, and Port St. Lucie, utilizing road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. Sheriff John Budensiek described how deputies tracked Daceus through the area. He runs through the neighborhood, runs through several yards. Our deputies, including canine deputies, get there. The neighbors are able to point to the last location they saw him running. They picked up a track, found his hat. We were able to track him through some really dense woods, through a backyard, and then into the swamp.

Resident Tanya Talanczuck said she sheltered in place during the search near Wind Stone. I closed my doors and I said I don't want him in my house. She said the heavy police presence caught her by surprise in what she called a very safe neighborhood. I'm glad they caught him so fast. I thought he'd get away. Budensiek said deputies pursued Daceus after he injured someone. Once he hurt one of our people, it was game on for us. I truly believe he would have done anything to get away. He did do anything he could possibly do to get away. So we felt that he was a danger to the community.

hero.body:
Repeated flooding on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach is raising concerns among business owners, and the city says a permanent fix could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete. Wednesday's storm flooded the street so severely that water reached knee height in the middle of the road, according to Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, who called it one of the worst floodings he has seen in 20 years.

 The flooding has become a recurring problem tied to daily afternoon thunderstorms. Ocean Drive also flooded on Monday. Aubrey Moxley, who works at Allure Gallery across the street, said the entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain this week. The flooding creates dangerous conditions for employees and threatens to cripple businesses by preventing customers from reaching the beach and shops along the strip.

 The City of Vero Beach Public Works Department said pump stations and drainage infrastructure are working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. Recent storms exceeded that capacity, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour. To fix the flooding, staff said the city would need to rebuild the road and make drainage improvements.

 The city has no improvement project planned for Ocean Drive at this time. Olsen expressed concern about what a major storm could bring to ground-level businesses along the street and questioned where the city draws the line between cost and damage to local businesses.

hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.

The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases at 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility's operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. Property owners receive 75 days notice before the charge takes effect.
